title: How To Eliminate Cell Phone Use In The Classroom sroom/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by watching A&E's Undercover High, Linsin lays out a detailed, school-wide policy for eliminating cell phone use in class, arguing that vague rules merely discouraging phone use are functionally meaningless. His policy bans phones (and visible headphones) from even being pulled out between the start and end of class, with no gray area or exceptions based on intent, and recommends immediate confiscation without a prior warning to avoid students burning through repeated free passes. He specifies practical mechanics: phones collected respectfully in a ziplock bag, returned at day's end, with escalating consequences—parent pickup, detention, administrative referral—for repeat offenses. He stresses that the policy only works if every teacher and administrator enforces it uniformly, and encourages individual teachers at schools without such a policy to organize colleagues and propose it formally, insisting that any school, regardless of size or culture, can successfully implement it if committed.
points: Vague policies merely discouraging cell phone use are functionally meaningless and unenforceable.
The recommended policy bans phones and visible headphones from being pulled out at all during class, with zero exceptions based on intent.
Confiscation should happen immediately without a prior warning, using a ziplock bag as a respectful, non-confrontational method.
Repeat offenses escalate to parent pickup, detention, and administrative referral to strengthen the policy over time.
Uniform, school-wide teacher and administrator buy-in is essential; a policy followed by only some staff quickly loses credibility.
quotes: Unless your content and ability to deliver it are more compelling than the highly addictive nature of cell phones, then learning will be profoundly and negatively affected.
Merely banning their use doesn’t go far enough and will only lead to arguing and battling with students over what, exactly, this means.
As for consequences, I recommend that phones be taken away without students first receiving a warning. Otherwise, they’ll use up their warning every chance they get.
By using a plastic bag rather than taking the phone by hand, it shows respect for the student’s property.
Everyone must buy in. Every teacher and administrator on campus must follow the policy as it’s written in the student handbook. Otherwise, it isn’t worth the paper it’s printed on.
It will work anywhere and at any school that commits to it and decides that enough is enough.
